rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some lexical patterns are kept intact because they do not follow a verb pattern; surrounding consonant quiescence also favors retention, as with gemination before a quiescent consonant.
rows.anchor: لأنه ليس على مثال الفعل فيمثل به ولكنه أتم لسكون ما قبله وما بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many derived noun patterns retain wāw or yāʾ rather than hamzating them; Sībawayh lists forms such as ʿawār, qawwāl, and miqwāl.
rows.anchor: وذلك فعل وفعال نحو حول وعوار وكذلك فعال نحو قوال ومفعال نحو مشوار

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs say abyanāʾ, with a quiescent yāʾ and a vowel on bāʾ to avoid kasra on yāʾ; Sībawayh says this is not regular.
rows.anchor: وقد قال بعض ~~العرب أبيناء فأسكن الياء وحرك الباء كره الكسرة في الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal nouns iqāma and istiqāma are defective because they remain closely tied to their derived verbs; as independent triliteral verbal nouns, they would retain the full form.
rows.anchor: الإقامة والاستقامة فإنما اعتلتا كما اعتلت أفعالهما لأن لزوم الاستفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive participle mafʿūl is shortened and made quiescent because it is the noun of its verb, so it follows the verb in defectiveness; other cited forms are not verb-nouns.
rows.anchor: وأما مفعول فإنهم حذفوه فيهما وأسكنوه لأنه الاسم من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭawīl is not formed on yaṭūlu; if it were the verb-based noun, it would be ṭāʾil. It instead patterns as faʿīl with a passive sense and preserves the root, as in makhyūṭ.
rows.anchor: فإن طويلا لم يجئ على يطول ولا على الفعل ألا ترى أنك لو أردت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maqāwil and maʿāyish are not hamzated because they are plurals of maqāla and maʿīša, whose original vowels remain; they are not nouns patterned on the verb.
rows.anchor: ولم يهمزوا مقاول ومعايش لأنهما ليستا بالاسم على الفعل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl explains that mafʿal is retained because it is essentially shortened from mifʿāl; the patterns share adjectival meaning and can alternate, as in maftaḥ and miftāḥ.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن مفعل لأي شيء أتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh calls maṣāʾib an error from treating maṣība as faʿīla; it is mafʿila, and maṣāwib is also attested.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنهم توهموا أن مصيبة فعيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The weak radicals in ʿajūz, risāla, and ṣaḥīfa are hamzated in their plurals because they are originally quiescent, unlike roots that take vowels; after alif they are especially liable to hamza.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن واو عجوز وألف رسالة وياء صحيفة لأي شيء همزن في الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʿil forms from ʿawirat and ṣīdat are ʿāwir and ṣāyid, preserving their weak radicals as in šawayt and ḥayiyt, though assimilation does not apply.
rows.anchor: فاعل من عورت فإذا قالوا فاعل غدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fawāʿil plurals from ʿawirat and ṣīdat take hamza by analogy with šawāyā and other hamzated plurals; the heavy meeting of two wāws also supports the change.
rows.anchor: فإذا قلت فواعل من عورت وصيدت همزت لأنك تقول في شويت شوايا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a noun is formed first and then pluralized, as in taqāwul and tabāyuʿ, hamza is not introduced: the weak radical was originally vowelled, as in maʿūna and maʿīša.
rows.anchor: لو كانت تقول اسما ثم أردت أن تكسر للجمع لقلة تقاول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fronted or postponed locative does not raise the noun: the noun remains a nominative subject, while the locative supplies its setting, as in fīhā ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: فعبد الله ارتفع بالابتداء لأن الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A locative before the subject can form a complete sentence, and an inna construction allows it to be shifted after the noun without changing its role.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى أنك لو قلت فيها عبد الله حسن السكوت وكان كلاما مستقيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the locative precedes a nominative predicate it may be ungoverning; with an accusative predicate it separates subject from predicate, and the subject licenses the circumstantial accusative.
rows.anchor: قد حالت بين المبتدإ والقائم واستغنى بها فعمل المبتدأ حين لم يكن القائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A locative can mark where a state holds while the predicate remains built on its subject, as in huwa laka khāliṣ or ʿAbd Allāh qāʾim fīhā.
rows.anchor: ومن قال فيها عبد الله قائم قال هو لك خالص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase khāliṣa yawma l-qiyāma is read with khāliṣa nominative or accusative; the accusative is more common because it functions like a verbal noun, khulūṣan.
rows.anchor: وقد قرى هذا الحرف على وجهين @QB@ قل هي للذين آمنوا في الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Predicates can precede a locative and be accusative as circumstantial modifiers; rajul ṣidq maʿlūman describes a fact in that state, while nominative can make the word adjectival.
rows.anchor: في الشعر قد انتصب خبره وهو مقدم قبل الظرف قوله

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl analyzes ḥasana ummuhu karīman abūhā as describing a quality established for the mother in that circumstance; nominative is also possible as an adjective.
rows.anchor: مررت برجل حسنة أمه كريما أبوها زعم الخليل أنه أخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afaʿala commonly makes an intransitive verb causative: dakhala, kharaja, and jalasa become adkhalahu, akhrajahu, and ajlasahu when another agent causes the action.
rows.anchor: تقول دخل وخرج وجلس فإذا أخبرت أن غيره صيره إلى شيء من هذا قلت أخرجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿala and afaʿala can sometimes share causative meaning, as in fariḥa/farriḥahu or afraḥahu, gharima/gharramahu or aghramahu, and similar pairs.
rows.anchor: وقد يجيء الشيء على فعلت فيشرك أفعلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms ṭaradtu and aṭradtu differ: the first means I drove him away, while the second means I made him a fugitive; hounds ṭaradna the game by driving it along.
rows.anchor: وأما طردته فنحيته وأطردته جعلته طريدا هاربا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭalaʿa means appeared, aṭlaʿa ʿalayhim means came upon them, šariqa means appeared, and ašraqa means shone; asraʿa means hastened and abṭaʾa means delayed.
rows.anchor: ويقال طلعت أي بدوت وطلعت الشمس أي بدت وأطلعت عليهم أي هجمت عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saraʿa and baṭuʾa describe inherent qualities like lightness and heaviness and are not transitive, unlike ṭawwaltu l-amr or ʿajjalته.
rows.anchor: غريزة كقولك خف وثقل ولا تعديهما إلى شيء كما تقول طولت الأمر وعجلته

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl says fatanahu and ḥazanahu mean putting temptation or grief into someone, like kaḥaltuhu and dahantuhu; making someone tempting or sad instead takes aftanahu or aḥzanahu.
rows.anchor: فتنته وحزنته لم ترد أن تقول جعلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shatara r-rajulu and shatarat ʿaynuhu are distinct formations; to make a man squint, use aštarahu, just as afzaʿahu differs from faziʿa.
rows.anchor: وشترت عينه فإذا أردت تغير شتر الرجل لم تقل إلا أشترته

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One group transmits Nuṣayb's poetic line with sawadtu, as in sawadtu fa-lam amlik sawādī.
rows.anchor: وقد اختلفوا في هذا البيت لنصيب ~~فقال بعضهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another group reads the line as suddat, interpreting it as a faʿalt form.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم ~~سدت يعني فعلت

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs use aftantu, aḥzantu, arjaʿtu, and aʿwartu ʿaynahu to mean making someone or something acquire that state.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض العرب أفتنت الرجل وأحزنته وأرجعته وأعورت عينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several verbs allow paired intransitive and transitive forms for putting a state into something, including jabara/jabartuhu and rakaḍat/rakaḍtu.
rows.anchor: جبرت يده وجبرتها وركضت الدابة وركضتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faʿalt causative meaning to make someone become something is rare; examples are faṭartuhu fa-afṭara and bashartuhu fa-abshara.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء فعلته إذا أردت أن تجعله مفعلا وذلك فطرته فأفطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khaṭṭaʾtuhu means called him a wrongdoer, like calling someone fāsiq or zānī; ḥayyaytuhu is a greeting, while saqaytuhu and raʿaytuhu can express a prayer for him.
rows.anchor: فأما خطأته فإنما أردت سميته مخطئا كما أنك

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Asqaytuhu is also used in the sense of saqaytuhu; Dhū al-Rumma's poem about watering the ruins illustrates this usage.
rows.anchor: معنى سقيته فدخلت على فعلت كما تدخل فعلت عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afaʿaltuhu can expose someone to an event, as in aqtaltuhu, exposed him to killing; qabartuhu means buried him, while aqbartuhu provided him a grave.
rows.anchor: على أن تعرضه لأمر وذلك قولك أقتلته أي عرضته للقتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqaytuhu means he drank what I gave; asqaytuhu means I provided water and a supply, paralleling kasawtuhu/albastuhu; shafaytuhu cures, while ashfaytuhu gives a cure.
rows.anchor: جعلت له ماء وسقيا ألا ترى أنك تقول أسقيته أي جعلت له ماء وسقيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afaʿala can mean acquiring a condition: ajraba, anḥaza, and aḥāla mean becoming affected by mange, wasting, or livestock loss; related forms describe a person who owns such traits or resources.
rows.anchor: وتقول أجرب الرجل وأنحز وأحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alāma r-rajulu means he became deserving of blame, whereas lāmahu means he reproached him; similar forms describe having abundant or scarce means.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك قول الرجل ألام الرجل أي صار صاحب لائمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣrama, amḍagha, aḥṣada, and ajazza describe crops that have become ready to be cut, chewed, or harvested; the simple verb reports actually doing the act.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذا أصرم النخل وأمضغ وأحصد الزرع وأجز النخل وأقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamidtu means I rewarded him and gave his due, whereas aḥmadtu means I found him deserving of praise, like crops becoming ready for cutting.
rows.anchor: وقالوا حمدته أي جزيته وقضيته حقه فأما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arāba means becoming a person of suspicion, while rābanī means causing suspicion in me; the distinction parallels becoming worthy of blame versus reproaching someone.
rows.anchor: وقالوا أراب كما قالوا ألام أي صار صاحب ريبة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl says some faʿalt/afʿalt pairs have the same meaning but differ by dialect, such as qalaltu/alqaltu, šaġaltu/ašġaltu, and bakartu/abkartu.
rows.anchor: زعم ذلك الخليل فيجيء به قوم على فعلت ويلحق قوم فيه الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh gives further synonymous dialect forms, including qalaltu/alqaltu, šaġaltu/ašġaltu, ṣarra/aṣarra, and bakara/abkara.
rows.anchor: قلته البيع وأقلته وشغله وأشغله وصر أذنيه وأصر أذنيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣbaḥnā, amsaynā, asḥarnā, and afjarnā mean entering those times of day; ṣabbaḥnā and similar simple forms mean visiting someone then.
rows.anchor: في حين صبح ومساء وسحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verbs such as yušajjaʿu, yujabbanu, and yuqawwā describe someone being labeled or charged with those qualities; šanuʿa can similarly be said of a person.
rows.anchor: وما بني على يفعل يشجع ويجبن ويقوى أي يرمي بذلك ومثله قد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghallaqa can describe repeated work closing many doors; aghlaqa is also good for plural doors, and al-Farazdaq's verse attests aghliqu abwāban.
rows.anchor: وقالوا أغلقت الباب وغلقت الأبواب حين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr distinguished nazaltu from anzaltu.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو عمرو أيضا يفرق بين نزلت وأنزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abāna and istabāna can be used with or without the added object form to mean that a thing became clear or that one made it clear, with paired forms sharing meaning.
rows.anchor: ويقال أبان الشيء نفسه وأبنته واستبان واستبنته والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms such as majnūn, maslūl, and mazqūm derive from underlying verbs like janantuhu or salaltuhu even when those verbs are unused; replacement verbs can make the unused forms unnecessary.
rows.anchor: وإنما جاءت هذه الحروف على جننته وسللته وإن لم يستعمل في الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Janna and salla can mean putting madness or illness into someone, like ḥazuna and raḏula; janantuhu means I put madness in you, parallel to aqbartuhu giving someone a grave.
rows.anchor: جعل فيه الجنون والسل كما قالوا حزن وفسل ورذل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary vocatives are introduced by five forms: yā, ayā, hayā, ay, or a final alif, as in yā Ḥār ibn ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: فأما الاسم غير المندوب فينبه بخمسة أشياء بيا وأيا وهيا وأى وبالألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four vocatives other than alif can prolong a call to someone far away, inattentive, or deeply asleep; these forms can serve where alif is used, but alif cannot serve in those cases.
rows.anchor: يستعملونها إذا أرادوا أن يمدوا أصواتهم للشئ المتراخى عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long forms can also address someone nearby for emphasis; all five markers may be omitted when the addressee is treated as present and directly addressed.
rows.anchor: كان صاحبك قريبا منك مقبلا عليك توكيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocative particle cannot be omitted with demonstratives because it replaces ay after its deletion; yā may be dropped with an indefinite in poetry, but Sībawayh calls this rare and weak.
rows.anchor: الحرف الذي ينبه به لزم المبهم كأنه صار بدلا من أي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj omits yā in the poetic address jāri, intending yā jāriya; Sībawayh treats such deletion as uncommon and weak.
rows.anchor: وقد يجوز حذف يا من النكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā is required with a person being implored or marveled at; lamentation uses yā and wā, with lengthening for a sung call to someone distant.
rows.anchor: وأما المستغاث به فيا ~~لازمة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In jītuka annaka, the construction means jītuka li-annaka: the lām is deleted before an; the deleted preposition makes the dependent construction accusative.
rows.anchor: تقول جئتك أنك تريد المعروف إنما أراد جئتك لأنك تريد المعروف ولكنك حذفت

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl parses Q 23:52 as if it said wa-li-anna hādhihi ummatukum; similarly, deleting the lām from li-īlāfi in Q 106:1 leaves an accusative construction for fa-li-yaʿbudū.
rows.anchor: هذا قول الخليل ولو قرءوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase in Q 23:52 can also be read with inna as a fresh clause, which Sībawayh says is good Arabic.
rows.anchor: ولو قلت جئتك إنك تحب المعروف مبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The annī clauses in Q 23:26 and Q 11:25 are understood as bi-annī; Sībawayh explains them as omitting the preposition bāʾ.
rows.anchor: أراد بأني مغلوب ~~وبأني لكم نذير مبين

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl reads wa-an al-masājida li-llāh as wa-li-an: because the mosques belong to God, worship none with Him; the lām analysis also explains the clause's relation to the governing verb.
rows.anchor: ولأن المساجد لله فلا تدعوا مع الله أحدا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators instead construe wa-an al-masājida as governed by ūḥiya, parallel to wa-annahu lammā qāma ʿabdu llāh yadʿūhu in Q 72:19; reading wa-inna is also possible.
rows.anchor: المفسرون فقالوا على أوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh favors Khalīl's lām analysis: its semantic relation to the verb permits fronting or postponing the clause, like other constituents linked through lām.
rows.anchor: المعنى معنى اللام فإذا كان الفعل أو غيره موصلا إليه باللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line manaʿtu Tamīman can be read either with an omitted lām or as a fresh inna clause; Sībawayh also heard an Arab say innī anā ibnuhā.
rows.anchor: قال الفرزدق # % منعت تميما منك أني أنا ابنها

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: For labbayka inna l-ḥamda, a genitive analysis after a deleted preposition is also strong, but Sībawayh identifies Khalīl's lām analysis as preferred, supported by wa-an al-masājida li-llāh.
rows.anchor: والأول قول الخليل ويقوي ذلك قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dual nouns take alif plus nūn in the nominative and yāʾ plus nūn in the accusative and genitive; ordinary non-defective, non-hamzated nouns form the dual by opening the final consonant.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن التثنية تكون في الرفع بالألف والنون وفي النصب والجر بالياء
